newsitem.title: CYPRUS: UK foreign minister jostled by Cyprus protesters.
newsitem.headline: UK foreign minister jostled by Cyprus protesters.

text.p: British Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind, on a mission to persuade Turkish and Greek Cypriots to open peace talks, on Sunday gained insight into the passions governing the divided island when he was confronted by Greek protesters.

The six elderly women, dressed in black and bearing photos of relatives they said had disappeared after Turkish troops invaded north Cyprus in 1974, advanced on Rifkind as he arrived for a reception and thrust leaflets in his hand.
The women pleaded with a bewildered Rifkind for help and then called out after the retreating minister: "Mr Malcolm, we only want human rights."
The protesters said around 1,500 Greek Cypriots were still missing after the invasion, while the Turks say about 800 of their community are still missing.

Rifkind had only arrived in Cyprus a few hours earlier in a bid to persuade the leaders of the Greek and Turkish communities that it was high time they buried decades of hostility and started peace talks.

"I have no illusions about the difficulties involved... we are all realistic and know progress won't happen overnight," said Rifkind, the first British Foreign Secretary to visit the divided eastern Mediterranian island for 30 years. Cyprus, once part of the Ottoman Empire, was a British colony from 1914 until independence in 1960.

Rifkind said the international community was increasingly concerned by an upsurge in violence over the last six months in which four people were killed in or near the buffer zone separating Turkish and Greek Cypriots.

"At a time when the Cold War is over, the Berlin Wall has fallen and apartheid is no more, surely it is not unrealistic that this small beautiful island can find a peace and justice acceptable to all," he told reporters on arrival in Cyprus.
The United Nations has been trying without success for decades to broker a settlement but the international community has come to the conclusion that the Cyprus problem cannot be allowed to fester.

U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said last week that the situation on the island was the worst since Turkish troops invaded and occupied the northern third in 1974 after a coup engineered by the military regime then ruling Greece.
"It is of the utmost importance that we find a workable solution...we've lived with the consequences far too long," Cypriot Foreign Minister Alecos Michaelides told reporters.
"I am optimistic that 1997 might be the year for Cyprus."
A British official said the first round of talks between Rifkind and Michealides had passed off well and that the discussions would become more detailed later on Sunday.
Rifkind, speaking earlier on board his plane, said the international community could not afford to dawdle.

"As we've seen over the last few months, the lack of a political settlement means that even the smallest incident has led to serious loss of life. The situation is not stable -- it could descend into serious conflict," he said.

The Turkish Cypriots, whose self-declared state is only recognised by Ankara, have around 35,000 Turkish and Turkish Cypriots troops. The Cypriot National Guard has 11,500 troops but recently acquired 77 Russian and French battle tanks.
Both Turkey and Greece have defence pacts with their respective communities on the island.
British officials are optimistic that Greek Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash will hold face-to-face talks in the next six months.

One possible key to talks is Cyprus's desire to open talks on European Union membership and Rifkind said it would be much easier for the island to gain entry to the EU if a political settlement was reached first.
